title: Vaccines that elicit broad protection against hypervariable viruses

concept.text: The proposed innovation is vaccination that produces durable protection against viruses whose diversity makes broad protection difficult. Its central design idea is to direct human immunity toward conserved viral sites: features shared across otherwise different strains that offer useful targets for protection. HIV and influenza are the principal examples in this record. The intended outcome is protection against diverse exposures, rather than an immune response that recognizes only a narrow selection of vaccine-matched strains.

In the proposed antibody-based approach, vaccination would guide the development of broadly neutralizing antibodies capable of blocking diverse viral strains. Starting an appropriate B-cell lineage, developing that lineage into a sufficiently broad and potent antibody response, maintaining the response, and demonstrating clinical protection are separate milestones. A response to a conserved target is therefore a design achievement, but does not by itself establish prevention of infection. This explanation synthesizes the supplied concept and review; the supplied sources do not independently document the full mechanism.

The concept contains two distinct clinical ambitions: prevention of HIV acquisition across diverse circulating strains, and influenza protection that persists across seasons and extends to mismatched variants or subtypes. Both belong to the same broader goal of overcoming viral variability, but success against either virus would establish only that achievement. It would not establish that one vaccine or one immunogen-design method solves both problems.

significance.text: If achieved, durable vaccination-based prevention of HIV acquisition would provide a major additional means of preventing infection. Broad influenza protection lasting across several seasons could reduce dependence on repeated vaccine reformulation and improve protection when circulating viruses differ from those represented in a vaccine. These are conditional consequences of the proposed capability; their magnitude would depend on efficacy, duration, safety, uptake and the breadth actually demonstrated.

Influenza protection against selected mismatched subtypes would be consequential, but would not establish protection against every possible pandemic subtype. Protection against seasonal drift and protection across subtypes are related but distinct dimensions of breadth, and each needs appropriate evidence. Likewise, preventing infection, reducing symptomatic illness and preventing severe disease are different outcomes. A vaccine could deliver substantial clinical benefit without preventing every infection, but its claims would need to identify the outcome demonstrated.

As a conditional extension of the design idea, success could inform vaccines against hepatitis C or future coronavirus spillovers. Such applications would require separate development and validation because conserved targets, accessible immune responses and protective mechanisms can differ between viruses. A successful HIV or influenza vaccine would provide an example to build on, rather than establish a general solution for all rapidly changing viruses.

The conceptual distinction from long-acting antiviral prophylaxis is the source of protection: vaccination seeks to establish a protective immune response, whereas prophylaxis relies on administered drug exposure. Either approach can contribute to prevention. This record provides no basis for assuming that vaccination would automatically achieve wider access, eliminate repeat dosing or replace pharmaceutical prevention.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is reliable induction of an immune response that is simultaneously broad enough to cover diverse viruses, potent enough to protect people, and durable enough to remain useful over time. Conserved-site recognition alone is insufficient if the response cannot block infection or deliver the specified clinical benefit. The supplied research identifies this as the missing capability, but the available review does not establish whether every component remains unsolved as of November 1, 2026.

Within the proposed antibody strategy, the engineering challenge is to connect immunogen design to a complete protective response: recruit suitable precursor B cells, guide their development toward broader neutralization, and sustain effective responses. Concrete questions include whether conserved sites can be presented in a form that induces useful antibodies, whether competing responses divert development, and whether a practical vaccination schedule can produce sufficient breadth and durability. These are design challenges synthesized from the supplied material, rather than findings independently verified from the indexed sources.

The original research attributes the difficulty partly to immune responses being dominated by hypervariable surfaces. That mechanism remains a hypothesis in this record because the review had no supporting source text with which to assess its scope. The broader problem can still be stated without treating that assertion as settled: a vaccine must elicit protection that survives meaningful viral variation. For HIV and influenza, the relevant targets, exposure patterns and clinical endpoints must be evaluated separately.

current_state.text: The supplied research attributes to the December 2025 Lancet HIV report on HVTN 706/HPX3002/Mosaico a vaccine-efficacy estimate of −0.7% over months 7–24, with a 95% confidence interval of −50.9% to 32.8% and p=0.97, and reports that the mosaic regimen did not demonstrate prevention of HIV-1 acquisition. These figures are retained as reported, rather than independently verified: the source index contains an abstract URL but no captured text or artifacts, and the validated review could not check the estimate, analysis details or conclusion. The reported point estimate should not be interpreted as establishing increased infection risk; the reported interval spans both negative and positive efficacy.

The supplied research also attributes to the U.S. Government Accountability Office’s May 22, 2025 spotlight a count of eight early trials of universal vaccine candidates that started or finished between January 2015 and April 2025, with none having reached the market. The review could not verify the count, exact candidate scope, time window or market-status wording because no source text was captured. This is therefore a dated account attributed to GAO, not an exhaustive trial census or a verified statement of market availability in November 2026.

The research describes early human studies as capable of inducing some broadly neutralizing-antibody precursors. No specific study or inspectable passage was supplied for that assertion, so it remains an unverified account of an intermediate milestone. Even if confirmed, precursor induction would not establish successful maturation into durable protective immunity or clinical efficacy. Conversely, the absence of supporting artifacts here is not evidence that precursor induction has not occurred.

The supplied record does not support a complete historical judgment that every HIV vaccine efficacy trial has failed, nor a definitive present-day claim that no efficacious HIV or universal influenza vaccine exists. Its review contains no substantive freshness search through November 1, 2026. Consequently, the dated results above describe the progress reported in the supplied research, while subsequent developments and the current frontier remain unassessed. No preprint designation or scientific dispute is established by these materials; the principal limitation is unavailable source text and incomplete verification.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration for HIV: a randomized efficacy trial in a population with sufficient HIV incidence to evaluate acquisition shows clinically meaningful, durable protection, with the efficacy estimate, uncertainty and follow-up reported. The protocol should prespecify what counts as adequate protection and duration, and characterize the viral diversity encountered. No numerical efficacy percentage is adopted here as an authoritative cutoff. Antibody measurements and precursor induction would support interpretation but would not substitute for the proposed acquisition endpoint.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized HIV trial demonstrates clinically meaningful, durable protection against acquisition

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration for influenza: a candidate protects across several seasons against explicitly identified mismatched influenza A variants and subtypes without annual strain replacement during the demonstration period. The trial program should prespecify whether the principal endpoint is infection, symptomatic disease or severe disease, and document the circulating viruses and vaccine–virus relationships. Results should distinguish protection within a subtype from protection across subtypes. Several successful seasons would establish the breadth and durability observed, not literal universality or coverage of all future pandemic viruses.
completion_criteria.label: Multiseason protection against mismatched influenza A subtypes without strain replacement

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: convincing evidence would include independent confirmation or consistent results across trials, relevant populations and settings; transparent assessment of waning protection; and safety evidence appropriate to preventive use. Dose schedules, manufacturing consistency and the feasibility of delivery would help determine practical value. These are proposed evaluation dimensions, not established regulatory standards supplied by the sources. Protection demonstrated only in selected populations or under a demanding regimen should be described within those boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible protection with reported safety, waning and practical boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Under the supplied candidate’s proposed combined criterion, both the HIV and influenza demonstrations would be needed to complete the full ambition represented by this record. They should nevertheless be evaluated and reported separately: success against one virus would be a major achievement without completing the other. This combined requirement is an organizing proposal for CLM-10, not a requirement attributed to the indexed publications.
completion_criteria.label: Both HIV and influenza demonstrations completed and reported separately

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with CLM-01, “Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance”: both seek precise control over responses to particular antigens. CLM-10 aims to establish protective antiviral immunity, while CLM-01 aims to establish tolerance to selected targets. Shared interest in antigen selection and immune programming does not make these interchangeable outcomes.

Conceptual comparison with CLM-02, “Clearance of persistent viral reservoirs that force lifelong therapy”: both concern durable control of viral disease, particularly relevant to HIV. CLM-10’s proposed HIV endpoint is prevention of acquisition; CLM-02 addresses reservoirs after persistent infection is established. Preventing new infection would not demonstrate reservoir clearance, and clearing reservoirs would not demonstrate vaccination-based protection against future acquisition.

Conceptual comparison with CLM-09, “Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver”: both could involve directing a biological intervention toward a precisely defined target, but their defining outcomes differ. CLM-10 concerns protection elicited by vaccination; CLM-09 concerns therapeutic genome writing. A future overlap in delivery or biological engineering would not merge the concepts or make evidence for one sufficient for the other.

These comparisons are synthesis from the supplied roster, which provides titles rather than detailed records for the other concepts. CLM-10 principally belongs to vaccine development and clinical prevention, with contributions from immunology, structural biology and virology. Its relationship to the roster’s other organ repair, cancer, aging, pain, screening and transfusion concepts is broad biomedical relevance rather than a shared completion criterion; those entries remain separate.

unresolved_issues: The Mosaico numerical results, analysis population, endpoint definition and publication details remain unchecked because no captured source text or artifacts were supplied.
The GAO count of eight trials, exact candidate scope, reporting window and market-status statement remain unverified.
No specific source supports the reported human broadly neutralizing-antibody precursor milestone or the asserted dominance of responses to hypervariable surfaces.
Developments after the dated source accounts, including whether the target capability remains open as of November 1, 2026, were not assessed in the supplied review.
The proposed trials still require prespecified efficacy and duration targets, influenza endpoints, subtype coverage, populations and follow-up; no authoritative numerical threshold is supplied.
Requiring both HIV and influenza success remains a proposed combined completion rule rather than a source-established standard.
Detailed overlap with roster entries beyond their supplied titles cannot be assessed without their individual concept records.

brief.title: Vaccines that protect against widely varying viruses
possible: People could gain lasting protection against HIV infection despite differences between circulating strains. Influenza vaccination could protect across seasons, including against viruses that differ from those used to make the vaccine.
These vaccines would train immunity to attack shared viral features. The proposed approach would build antibodies, immune proteins that block viruses, capable of working against many strains.
why: Durable HIV vaccination would add another way to prevent infection. Longer-lasting influenza protection could reduce repeated vaccine reformulation and improve protection when circulating viruses differ from the vaccine.

sources.showed: A clinical trial report on the effectiveness and safety of an HIV vaccine course.
sources.cited_for: The Mosaico vaccine course did not demonstrate prevention of HIV infection.
sources.not_established: The trial did not establish durable protection against diverse HIV strains.

sources.showed: A report surveying early trials of vaccines intended to protect broadly against varying viruses.
sources.cited_for: Vaccine candidates intended to provide broad protection had entered early trials.
sources.not_established: Early trials do not establish lasting clinical protection across diverse viral strains.

shown: The Mosaico HIV vaccine trial reported no demonstrated protection against infection. The U.S. Government Accountability Office described early trials of vaccine candidates intended to provide broad protection.
missing: Vaccination must produce antibodies that block diverse strains strongly enough and for long enough to protect people.
An HIV trial must demonstrate durable prevention of infection across diverse circulating strains.
Influenza trials must demonstrate protection across seasons and mismatched subtypes without annual strain replacement.
Protection must hold up across trials and populations, with suitable safety and a practical vaccination schedule.

milestones.label: Durable prevention of HIV infection in a randomized trial
milestones.explanation: A trial randomly assigning people to vaccination or comparison groups would have to show meaningful, lasting prevention of HIV infection across diverse strains. This would establish protection beyond antibody measurements.

milestones.label: Influenza protection across seasons and mismatched virus groups
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to show protection across seasons against mismatched influenza A subtypes, distinct groups of the virus, without annual strain replacement. This would establish the breadth and duration actually achieved.

milestones.label: Repeatable protection with clear safety and practical limits
milestones.explanation: Independent confirmation or consistent trials would have to establish protection, safety, how protection fades, and workable delivery. This would define who benefits and under what conditions.

milestones.label: HIV and influenza successes demonstrated separately
milestones.explanation: Both the HIV and influenza demonstrations would have to succeed and be reported separately. Success against either virus would complete that achievement while leaving the other ambition open.

uncertain: Can vaccination guide early antibody-producing cells into a broad, potent response that lasts?
What protection level and duration should count, and should influenza trials measure infection, illness or severe disease?
How much viral diversity and population diversity would trials need to cover to justify broad protection claims?

page.title: Broadly protective HIV and influenza vaccines
page.definition: One preventive vaccine reduces the risk of acquiring HIV-1 after exposure to genetically diverse circulating strains. A separate vaccine reduces the risk of symptomatic influenza from viruses in both groups of influenza A for at least one year. Groups 1 and 2 are the two evolutionary branches of haemagglutinin, a protein on the virus surface. Influenza B is a secondary target.

goal.need: An estimated 1.2 million people acquired HIV worldwide in 2025 (uncertainty range 950,000–1.7 million). A durable vaccine could give people who struggle to return for preventive medication another way to avoid infection. Seasonal influenza A and B together cause 3–5 million severe illnesses each year. Broader protection against influenza A could prevent illness when circulating strains differ from those selected for the seasonal vaccine. Fewer vaccinations would depend on protection lasting across seasons.

completion.title: Licensed HIV and influenza vaccines meet their separate clinical protection criteria.
completion.criterion: A national regulator licenses an HIV-1 vaccine for prevention of acquisition, supported by clinical protection against genetically diverse circulating strains. Separately, a licensed influenza vaccine meets NIAID's universal-vaccine criteria: at least 75% efficacy against symptomatic influenza infection, protection against group 1 and group 2 influenza A viruses, protection lasting at least 1 year, and suitability for all age groups. Each case is assessed separately; completion of this entry requires both. No numerical HIV breadth or durability threshold is specified.
completion.set_by: Atlas composite of national vaccine licensure and NIAID's 2018 influenza criteria; no external body sets the combined HIV–influenza test.
completion.threshold_quote: Be at least 75% effective against symptomatic influenza virus infection
completion.basis: Figure 2 of NIAID’s 2018 strategic plan defines the influenza efficacy, breadth, duration and age criteria. National regulators decide licensure for each product. The Atlas requires both licences and clinical evidence of cross-strain protection for HIV-1. AVAC’s 2025 agenda identifies an updated field-wide HIV vaccine target product profile as an unmet need.

milestones.title: A vaccine candidate elicits an immune response in animals.
milestones.criterion: An animal study shows that vaccination elicits an immune response to a vaccine antigen. CDC specifies no numerical antibody titre for this stage.
milestones.set_by: CDC, the proof-of-concept stage in How Vaccines are Developed and Approved for Use; a qualitative development criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: researchers study its ability to cause an immune response with small animals, like mice.

milestones.title: A vaccine candidate elicits an immune response in a phase 1 human study.
milestones.criterion: A regulator-authorized phase 1 study demonstrates a vaccine-induced immune response in volunteers and assesses safety and dose.
milestones.set_by: WHO, How are vaccines developed and produced?, phase 1 clinical-development convention.
milestones.threshold_quote: confirm it generates an immune response, and determine the right dosage.

milestones.title: A vaccine candidate elicits measured immune responses in a controlled phase 2 study.
milestones.criterion: A controlled phase 2 study characterizes the vaccine-induced immune response in people with characteristics of the intended recipients and assesses common short-term adverse effects.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Vaccine Development – 101, phase 2 development objectives; no common numerical immune-response pass mark is supplied.
milestones.threshold_quote: examine the relationship between the dose administered and the immune response

milestones.title: A phase 3 trial meets its prespecified test of clinical vaccine efficacy.
milestones.criterion: A controlled phase 3 trial meets its prespecified efficacy criterion against HIV-1 acquisition or symptomatic, laboratory-confirmed influenza in the specified population and follow-up period. For Mosaico, the lower 95% confidence bound had to exceed 20% for efficacy against HIV-1 acquisition from month 7 to month x (24 ≤ x ≤ 30) in the per-protocol population. For BVX-010, the lower two-sided 95% bound had to exceed 40% in the primary per-protocol analysis of PCR- or culture-confirmed influenza with protocol-defined influenza-like illness from 14 days after dose 2 through the first season.
milestones.set_by: Each trial’s protocol and statistical analysis plan specify its success rule, following ICH E9, section 2.1.2. Mosaico and BVX-010 provide the two numerical examples.
milestones.threshold_quote: A confirmatory trial is an adequately controlled trial in which the hypotheses are stated in advance and evaluated.

milestones.title: A national regulator begins reviewing a broadly protective vaccine for licensure.
milestones.criterion: The sponsor submits a licensing application for the preventive indication, and the national regulator begins its assessment of vaccine quality, safety and efficacy. In the United States, the Biologics License Application includes the preclinical and clinical evidence and information on the manufacturing process and facilities.
milestones.set_by: WHO’s description of national regulatory assessment and FDA’s Biologics License Application process.
milestones.threshold_quote: a vaccine must be assessed by the relevant regulatory body

not_found: No external combined HIV–influenza completion standard or current consensus numerical HIV breadth/duration target was found.

results.detail: The titre is pooled across the oral and parenteral vaccine arms. The study also included 10 unvaccinated controls.
results.quote: The protein immunization boosted these responses strongly in both groups to a titer of about 26,345 (geometric mean considering both groups) which contracted by ~6-fold over 10 weeks by the time of challenge.

results.finding: After HA stem vaccination, sera from mice (n=10 per group) and ferrets (n=6 per group) neutralized all 5 influenza A pseudoviruses tested.
results.detail: The vaccine combined H1 and H10 HA stem antigens. In the macaques (n=3), serum neutralization of H3N2 was detectable in the pseudovirus assay and below detection in the reporter-virus microneutralization assay.
results.quote: Mouse and ferret immune sera neutralized all 5 pseudotyped viruses that represent group 1 and group 2 human influenza viruses

results.finding: In a 45-person phase 1 trial, intramuscular BPL-1357 elicited an H7 serum IgG response in 85.7% of 14 evaluable recipients.
results.detail: The study compared administration routes at a single dose level, leaving dose–response unassessed.
results.quote: IM BPL-1357 induced higher serum IgG titers against H3, H5, and H7 relative to placebo, with 71.4%, 71.4%, and 85.7% of participants demonstrating a response.

results.finding: fH1/DSP-0546LP phase 1 trial (144 adults total) found a 10.37-fold rise in H1N1 neutralizing activity by day 29.
results.detail: The 144 participants were enrolled across all arms. The 10.37-fold rise is specific to the arm receiving 8 μg fH1 plus 5 μg DSP-0546LP, whose sample size is unspecified.
results.quote: In addition, exploratory analyses of the neutralizing activity of the induced antibodies against the H1N1 strain A/California/7/2009 showed GMFRs from Day 1 to Day 29 of 10.37-fold in the Formulation group receiving fH1 8 μg/DSP-0546LP 5 μg and 6.93-fold in the antigen-only formulation group receiving fH1 8 μg.

results.finding: In HVTN204 (480 randomized), the multiclade HIV-1 vaccine elicited ELISpot T-cell responses in 70.8% of 192 evaluable vaccine recipients.
results.quote:
T-cell responses, detected by interferon- c (IFN-c) ELISpot to global
potential T-cell epitopes (PTEs) were observed in 70.8% (136/192) of vaccine recipients overall

results.finding: ALVAC-HIV plus AIDSVAX B/E met its primary HIV-1 acquisition efficacy test in 16,395 participants (P = 0.04).
results.detail: The primary analysis excluded seven participants with HIV-1 at baseline. It was prespecified in the final analysis plan approved five months before unblinding. Reported P values were two-sided and unadjusted for multiple testing.
results.quote: the vaccine efficacy was 31.2% (95% CI, 1.1 to 52.1; P = 0.04).

results.finding: BVX-010 (M-001, n=12,458) had a crude vaccine efficacy of −15.9% against symptomatic, laboratory-confirmed influenza A or B.
results.detail: The crude efficacy is calculated as 1 − 160/138 because the two arms had equal denominators. The registry reports the case counts.

definition = "One preventive vaccine reduces the risk of acquiring HIV-1 after exposure to genetically diverse circulating strains. A separate vaccine reduces the risk of symptomatic influenza from viruses in both groups of influenza A for at least one year. Groups 1 and 2 are the two evolutionary branches of haemagglutinin, a protein on the virus surface. Influenza B is a secondary target.". Reason: The revision makes the two clinical outcomes explicit and identifies influenza B as a secondary target.

goal.need = "An estimated 1.2 million people acquired HIV worldwide in 2025 (uncertainty range 950,000\u20131.7 million). A durable vaccine could give people who struggle to return for preventive medication another way to avoid infection. Seasonal influenza A and B together cause 3\u20135 million severe illnesses each year. Broader protection against influenza A could prevent illness when circulating strains differ from those selected for the seasonal vaccine. Fewer vaccinations would depend on protection lasting across seasons.". Reason: The current rationale omits the scale of severe influenza, the difficulty of sustaining HIV prevention, and what broader protection would change for people exposed to either virus.

add statement by Coordinating Committee of the Global HIV/AIDS Vaccine Enterprise, 2005: "broadly reactive and persistent immune responses against HIV strains circulating in different parts of the world.". Reason: The Enterprise’s strategic plan explicitly calls for HIV vaccine responses that persist and recognize strains circulating in different regions.

add statement by UN Millennium Project, Working Group on HIV/AIDS, 2005: "research on vaccines must remain a high priority". Reason: The working group’s assessment documents both its support for HIV vaccine research and its reservation about achieving broad coverage with one vaccine.
